title: Not compassion, but service
hookLine: Ramakrishna stops mid-sentence: not compassion, but service, to every being as God
carry: seva: serve each person as God

lines: COMPASSION? WHO ARE YOU TO PITY?
NOT COMPASSION. SERVICE, AS TO GOD.
cards: Dakshineswar, the temple garden by the river where Ramakrishna lived. One day, in the telling of Saradananda, one of his monks, the talk turns to an old devotional teaching: show compassion to all creatures.
Ramakrishna slips into a deep mood and repeats the word. Compassion. Then he stops himself.
Compassion? Who are you, so small, to show compassion? No.
Not compassion. Service, to every being, as God.

teach.b: Young Narendra was in the room. He came out of the room and told the others he'd heard something wonderful, and that if he ever got the chance, he'd tell the world. Years later, as Swami Vivekananda, he did.

Karma Yoga is a set of his talks on work, and a chapter called We Help Ourselves, Not the World starts by letting the air out of the helper. The world isn't waiting for any one of us to rescue it, he says.
It will go on, with or without our help. So helping isn't a favor we do the world. It's a chance we're given.
He calls the world a great moral gymnasium, where we exercise to grow strong. Don't stand over someone and say, here, poor fellow, take this. Be thankful they let you give.
The blessing is to the giver. Then his teacher's words come back: serve the person in front of you as you would worship God, because, as Ramakrishna saw it, God is truly present in them.
Hindus call this seva: service offered as worship.
It's why the order he founded, the Ramakrishna Mission, runs schools, hospitals and relief work, under a motto that means, roughly: for your own freedom, and for the good of the world. Both at once.
So a Hindu at a food table isn't the rescuer. She's at worship. And the person taking the plate isn't a project.
They're the one she bows to, and the one who let her grow.

how: Hindu temples and service groups, including the Ramakrishna Mission, describe their kitchens, clinics and relief work as seva, service offered as worship, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

o: a set of stretches done before morning prayers
the path of work, offered as service and as worship
a rule that good work must always be thanked

games.q: not compassion, but service — tap the pairs.
p: not compassion, but service as to God
goes on with or without our help
where we exercise to grow stronger

s: Ramakrishna told his disciples to pity the poor from above
he stopped at 'compassion': not pity, but service to every being as God.
Vivekananda said the giver should be thankful to the one who receives
the blessing, he says, is to the giver.
Vivekananda said the world depends on our help
he said it goes on with or without us; helping is our chance to grow.

games.q: you've just served someone a plate at the temple, and they walk off without a word of thanks. what does seva ask of you?
o: thank them, and see God in them.
stop serving people who don't say thanks.
games.why: Ramakrishna's line: not compassion, but service to every being as God. in Vivekananda's picture, the one you serve is doing you the kindness.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've helped lately, a coworker, a parent, a stranger, a child, and notice if any part of you is still waiting for their thanks or keeping a small score. No need to scold that part.

Just turn it around, the way Ramakrishna did: see the one you helped as someone God is present in, and silently thank them for letting you serve. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know.

wordCard.voice: Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and Vivekananda's book of talks on it, where service is worship and the giver is the one who says thank you.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the yoga of action, the path Vivekananda's book describes.

carryVoice: Your line: seva, serve each person as God. The giver says thank you. Tomorrow, a fly finds a pot of honey. That's day nine hundred forty-two.
